title: Speech movements in MRI
Why speech is a remarkable learned skill
sourceText:
Speech and Language

• You learn to move your speech organs in
  extremely complex way with neither instructions,
  nor hardly any visual feedback.
• By 2-4 you can speak with a wide vocabulary and
  near-adult language, with hardly any explicit
  instruction.
• You may have also memorized the visual shape
  of the alphabet, but reading and writing whole
 wordscomes at 6-7, and requires a great deal of
  instruction.
• Articulatory Phonetics is the field that studies the
 movements of different vocal tract structures.
• And the last two year Voice Assistants and other
 Speech Tech have come to emulate the speech
  ability in ways none of us thought possible.
• Ling 285 is about Human and AI speech

title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters
sourceText:
AI: Ughhhhhh… Can’t we just ignore
AI?
• Given all we know about the psychological, economic, social, and
 environmental harm, can we just ignore AI– just pretend it doesn’t
  exist?
• Given the existential harm that many scientists warn about, can we just
 pretend it doesn’t exist?
• It exists, with many harms, and some benefits (e.g., immunotherapy,
 and yes, environmental engineering)
• One of the biggest dangers: We have no idea how it works. We know
  everything, and Understand nothing.
• And the people who know how it operates are very very few.
• In my opinion, AI literacy is necessary for scientists who use it,
  politicians who need to control it, lawyers who litigate on it, etc.
• I teach this course, because I believe that someone in a class like this, a

  benefit from them, while avoiding their negative consequences

title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern
sourceText:
Yt “cLOZE PROCEDURE” IS A NEW PSY-
chological tool for measuring the effec-
tiveness of communication. The meth-
od is straightforward; the data are
easily quantifiable; the findings seem to
stand up.

At the outset, this tool was looked
on as a new approach to “readability.”
It was so used in three pilot studies and
two experiments, the main findings of
which are reported here.

*Tho writer is particularly obligated to Prof.
Charles E. Osgood, University of Illinois, and
Melvin R. Marks, Personnel Research Section,
A.G.O., Department of the Army, for instigating
and assisting in the series of efforts that yielded
the notion of “cloze procedure.” Both are ex-
perimental psychologists. Among others who have
advised, encouraged or otherwise aided are these
of the University of Illinois: Prof. Lee J. Cron-
bach, educational psychologist and statistician;
Dean Wilbur Schramm, Division of Communica-
tions; Prof. Charles E. Swanson, Institute of
Communications Research, and George R. Klare,
psychologist, both of whom have authored arti-
cles on readability; and several journalism teach-
ers who lent their classes. Kalmer EB. Stordahl
and Clifford M. Christensen, until recently. re-
search associates of the Institute, also contributed.

First, the results of the new method
were repeatedly shown to conform with
the results of the Flesch and Dale-Chall
devices for estimating readability. Then
the scope broadened, and cloze proce-
dure was pitted against those standard
formulas.

If future research substantiates the
results so far, this tool seems likely to
have a variety of applications, both
theoretical and practical, in other fields
involving communication functions.

THE “CLOZE UNIT”

At the heart of the procedure is a
functional unit of measurement tenta-
tively dubbed a “cloze.” It is pro-
nounced like the verb “close” and is de-
rived from “closure.” The last term is
one gestalt psychology applies to the
human tendency to complete a familiar
but not-quite-finished pattern—to “see”
a broken circle as a whole one, for ex-
ample, by mentally closing up the gaps.

title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent
sourceText:
Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)
• What’s the average, the essence, of: [78,67,98,85,76,68,98,72]?
     • 1) Pick any random number x as the estimate of average, and we will improve it
     by observation. We are at time 0 in the algorithm. Let’s say the random number
    we pick is 130: x[0] = 130.
     • 2) Randomly pick a number d from the data, so we can see how far the data is
     from the estimate, as the average should be close to the data. Let’s say we pick d[0]
     = 98.
     • 3) x[0] = 130 and d[0] = 98. The mistake we’ve made is Loss = 130 – 98 = 32.
     • 4) Now let’s improve the estimate by reducing the discrepancy mistake = Loss by
      subtracting a bit of the Loss, let’s say 10% from the current estimate.
            •  x[1] = x[0] - 10% of 32
            •  x[1] = 130 – 3.2 = 126.8
     • 5) Repeat: Now pick another number d from the data to improve x from x[1] to
       x[2].
• What have we done? 1) Made an intial estimate/guess, 2) Used data to
 improve the estimate.
• Stochastic (Random) Gradient (Loss-related) Descent (reduce)

title: Position-first updates keep the oscillator bounded
speakerNotes:
Begin with x = [1] and v = [0]. In Slide Show, press Right Arrow once for each new pair of plotted values and list entries. There are 12 clicks after the initial state.

Numerical assumptions: k/m = 1 and dt = 0.5. At each step, perform x_new = x_old + dt*v_old, followed by v_new = v_old - dt*x_new. This is position-first symplectic Euler. It is an approximate oscillator, not exact cosine/sine samples and not simultaneous forward Euler. The update order matters. Each label and list displays three decimal places, but later steps use full precision. Initial list entries use the requested integers 1 and 0.

v = [0.0]
dt = 0.5
for step in range(12):
    x.append(x[-1] + dt*v[-1])
    v.append(v[-1] - dt*x[-1])

On the first click, x remains 1.000 and v becomes -0.500. On the second click, x becomes 0.750 and v becomes -0.875.

title: Template matching and successive representations
sourceText:
Templatic Perception and Hierarchical
Perception
• Our Goal: Understand how an NN uses its weights to process the
 input to make the right decision at the output, e.g., when given a
  [z] speech signal (= waveform = pressure waveform), the correct
 decision should be [z], not [s], not [a], etc.
• Something useful to know is how humans perceive speech,
  faces, etc. And perhaps knowing how how our own biological
 neural networks perceive speech, we can use that to understand
 how NNs model this via an artificial computation.
• So there are two basic theories of animal perception that inform
 NN design:
     • Templatic Perception
     • Hierarchical Perception

title: Templates make familiarity into a comparison
sourceText:
Templatic Perception

• Here’s a theory of how face perception works
     1.  The retina in the eye receives light information from the face
     2.  The brain has a template, a picture of sorts, stroed in it, of every face that the person knows
     3.  The brain compares the input face with each of its stored templates for faces
     4.  The template with the highest similarity to the input face is what is perceived
     5.    If there’s a name associated with the winning template, that name is the perceptual decision
• What this theory implies for AI: The knowledge weights of NNs are like perceptual
  templates.
• Remmber this from before: So the NN combines its currrent weights with the input
  face pixels and produces a Computed Output that is wrong (when we haven’t learnt
  anything)!
• So the way that an NN’s weights/knowledge/templates are combined with the input
  is that we determine similarity between weights and inputs.
• This is difficult to understand now, but just keep this in mind.

sourceText:

 known that
 perception is done in
  stages, hierarchically
• So the input leads to
 one new
  representation, then

 becomes another,

 output decision is

title: An inner product compares two numerical patterns
sourceText:
NNs are Templatic Hierarchical
Perceivers
•  Let’s first talk about the templatic aspect
• The key to templatic perception is that some internal template of numbers is compared to
  some input set of numbers to find out how similar the template is to the input
• NNs assume: Input is a list or vector of numbers and internal template weights are also a list
  or vector of numbers
• So how can we compare two lists of numbers to determine if they are similar or not.
•  E.g.
       •  Input = [-1 3 -2]
       • Temp1 = [-2 0 3]
       • Temp2 = [-2 2 -1]
•  Is list Input more similar to template 1 or 2?
• Inner product:
       •  Multiply 2 lists component-wise
       • Add all products
       •  If IP is near 0, the lists are dissimilar
       •  If IP is large and positive, lists are similar

Theory, Prediction, and Experiment




    • The Scientific Method depends on the statement of very clear theories about how the
    world is like, usually in the form of differential equations.

    • The differential equations are many of the type we have already seen, but slightly
    more complicated
    • Prediction: if I measure any of your laryngeal vibration signals, they will have a
    spectrum with equidistant harmonics.
    • Let’s do an experiment to find out if this is true!!!!!

title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
sourceText:
Principles of Mass-Spring Systems




   1.  Mass ↑ Frequency ↓, Stiffness ↑ Frequency ↓
   2.  An n-mass system has n modes of vibration, each with a higher frequency
   3.  An m’s increase lowers frequency proportionally to how much the mass moves,
      which depends on where it is!
   4.  Where there’s maximal movement, there’s no stretching, An where there’s maximal
        stretching, there’s no movement!
   5.  A k’s increase raises frequency proportionally to how much the spring
       stretches/compresses, which depends on where it is!
   6.   In a Fixed-Fixed System, the harmonics are multiples of the base frequency,
      because the base mode fits n-times into each successive mode
   7.   In a Fixed-Free System, the harmonics are odd multiples of the base frequency,
      because the base mode fits an odd n-times into each successive mode

title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
sourceText:
Principles of Mass-Spring Systems




   1.  Mass ↑ Frequency ↓, Stiffness ↑ Frequency ↓
   2.  An n-mass system has n modes of vibration, each with a higher frequency
   3.  An m’s increase lowers frequency proportionally to how much the mass moves,
      which depends on where it is!
   4.  Where there’s maximal movement, there’s no stretching, An where there’s maximal
        stretching, there’s no movement!
   5.  A k’s increase raises frequency proportionally to how much the spring
       stretches/compresses, which depends on where it is!
   6.   In a Fixed-Fixed System, the harmonics are multiples of the base frequency,
      because the base mode fits n-times into each successive mode
   7.   In a Fixed-Free System, the harmonics are odd multiples of the base frequency,
      because the base mode fits an odd n-times into each successive mode
